unit.title: Navigation and maps
unit.summary: Maps, contours, north, bearings and staying found, with the terrain flyover sim.

lessons.title: What a map is telling you
lessons.objective: You can read scale and legend to size up a route.

payload.prompt: A 1:24,000 map shows one inch equals how far?

explanation.correct: On a 1:24,000 scale map, one inch on the map is 24,000 inches in real life, which is about 2,000 feet. That's the standard USGS topo scale for day hikes.
explanation.incorrect: The ratio 1:24,000 means 24,000 real units per map unit: 24,000 inches divided by 12 is 2,000 feet. A 1:250,000 map is about 4 miles per inch.
explanation.sayThisLine: On a one-to-twenty-four-thousand map, one inch is two thousand feet.

payload.prompt: What does the map legend show you?
payload.template: The {{legend}} explains what each {{mark}} means, for example whether a dashed line is a {{trail}}.

explanation.correct: The legend is your decoder: it shows what each symbol, line color and pattern means. Dashed lines might be maintained trails, dotted lines might be rough routes. Different agencies use different symbols, so always check the legend first.
explanation.incorrect: Every map has a legend somewhere, usually in a corner. It tells you what the lines, colors and marks mean on that specific map.

payload.prompt: You have two maps of {{destination}}: 1:24,000 and 1:100,000. Which shows more detail?

options.text: The 1:100,000 scale is better for navigation

explanation.correct: Larger scale (smaller numbers) means more detail in a smaller area. A 1:24,000 map shows the same region with more zoomed-in detail than a 1:100,000 map. For day hiking, 1:24,000 is ideal.
explanation.incorrect: Smaller ratio numbers mean more zoomed in and more detail. A 1:24,000 quad covers about 6 by 8 miles; a 1:100,000 map covers roughly 30 by 40. Use 1:24,000 for hiking and 1:100,000 for planning.
explanation.sayThisLine: For hiking day trips, I use a one-to-twenty-four-thousand map. It has all the detail I need.

payload.prompt: Match the map concept to its role.

pairs.definition: The ratio of map distance to real-world distance
The key that explains what the map symbols and colors mean
A darker contour line usually every fifth line, labeled with elevation
Shows how true, magnetic and grid north differ where the map was made

distractorDefinitions: The date the map was printed
A list of trails in alphabetical order

explanation.summary: Every map has a scale, legend and declination diagram to orient you. The scale tells you distances, the legend decodes the symbols, and the diagram lets you match the map to a compass.
explanation.sayThisLine: Before you navigate, check the legend and the scale. They're your decoder.

facts.label: Your planned route
facts.value: A small local trail system you hiked five times

facts.label: Problem
facts.value: The trail junctions are too small to see clearly on the map

options.label: Get a 1:24,000 map; the detail will show each junction
options.consequence: A 1:24,000 map shows trails, junctions, water and terrain at a hiking scale, so you can match each junction you reach to the page.
considerations: Larger scale means more detail in a smaller area
Junctions are where people go wrong
Carry it as a paper map or a downloaded offline layer

options.label: Use a GPS track from a previous hike as your guide
options.consequence: A track shows a route someone walked, but not the other trails, junction choices or terrain around it. It is a good backup, not a replacement for a map.
considerations: Tracks can be wrong or out of date
Tracks do not show alternatives
Use a track and the map together

options.label: Use the 1:100,000 map; zoom in on your phone version
options.consequence: Zooming does not add detail; it only enlarges a coarse map. Small junctions stay invisible, and you may take a wrong turn.
considerations: Zoom does not add data
Phones can fail, so carry paper too
Pick a map made for hiking

payload.expertNote: A 1:24,000 USGS quad is the hiker's workhorse. It shows junctions, water, and terrain detail that a regional map can't. If you have a GPS track, it's good backup, but the map still matters.
payload.safetyNote: Always carry a paper map at the right scale. Zooming a low-detail map on a phone doesn't add detail; it just makes it blurry.
payload.prompt: Your regional map is too coarse to show local junctions. What now?

lessons.title: Contour lines 101
lessons.objective: You can read interval and index contours and find elevation on a map.

payload.prompt: Tap the index contour (the thick, dark line).

diagram.alt: A section of a topographic map showing contour lines at different elevations. One line is bold and labeled 8000 ft; the others nearby are thinner.

explanation.correct: Index contours are the bold, darker lines, usually every fifth regular contour. They are labeled with their elevation to help you orient quickly.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the thick lines that stand out from the thinner ones. Those bold lines are index contours and will have an elevation label nearby.

payload.prompt: A map says 'Contour interval 40 feet.' What does that mean?

options.text: The map covers 40 feet of elevation
Each contour line is 40 feet higher than the one below it
You climb 40 feet every time you cross a trail
The map scale is one inch per 40 feet

explanation.correct: Contour interval is the vertical distance between each contour line. If the interval is 40 feet, each line you cross means 40 feet of elevation change. If it's 80 feet (common on big terrain), each line is 80 feet.
explanation.incorrect: The interval is always printed on the map. Count the lines you will cross and multiply by the interval to estimate climbing. Lines packed close together mean that rise happens over a short distance, which is steep.
explanation.sayThisLine: Count the contours and multiply by the interval to find how much you'll climb.

payload.prompt: Contour lines packed close together: is that ground steep?

scene.alt: A topographic map with tightly packed contour lines on one side and widely spaced lines on the other.

explanation.correct: Tight contour lines mean a lot of elevation change in a small distance, which is steep. Spaced-out lines mean gentle terrain.
explanation.incorrect: If the lines are packed together you climb fast in a short distance. If they are spread apart, the same distance covers less elevation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Those contours are so tight the slope has to be brutal.

payload.prompt: Reading contour elevation.
payload.template: To find elevation, locate an {{index}}, read its {{number}}, then count regular contours {{up}} or down from it, multiplying by the interval.

explanation.correct: Index contours are your landmarks. Use them to orient yourself. Count contours from there, and the math tells you elevation at any spot on the map.
explanation.incorrect: Index contours are bold and labeled to make this easier. Find one, note its elevation, then count regular contours up or down from there.

facts.label: Question
facts.value: How much elevation gain on this leg?

options.label: Multiply: 15 lines × 80 feet = 1,200 feet of gain
options.consequence: Fifteen intervals of 80 feet is 1,200 feet, a solid climb worth planning time and water for.
considerations: Count the lines, then multiply by the interval
By Naismith's rule that is about 35 minutes of climbing time, before distance

options.label: Estimate 1,000 to 1,500 feet without the exact math
options.consequence: A rough range gets you close, but the multiplication is easy and gives a number you can actually plan with.
considerations: Estimates are fine for a quick look
Exact counts help with time and water

options.label: Say it's about 15 miles of climbing since you crossed 15 lines
options.consequence: Contour lines measure vertical distance, not miles. Mixing them up would badly distort your plan.
considerations: Lines are vertical steps
Miles come from the scale bar

payload.expertNote: Counting contours gives a fast net-gain check. Extra ups and downs along the way add more climbing than the net number, so pad your plan.
payload.safetyNote: Tightly packed contours mean steep ground. Plan extra time, and treat merged contours as a cliff to avoid.
payload.prompt: Your route crosses 15 contours on an 80-foot interval. How much climbing?

lessons.title: Contours come alive
lessons.objective: You can tell steep from gentle ground and spot cliffs from contour spacing.

payload.prompt: On a map, what do merged or very close contours signal?

options.text: A cliff or very steep wall

explanation.correct: When contour lines merge or bunch so tight you cannot see between them, that is a cliff or near-vertical wall. It is not a hiking route: go around it, and never try to climb it.
explanation.incorrect: Merged contours mean a lot of elevation in almost no horizontal distance, which is a cliff. Avoid these bands unless a marked route goes through them.
explanation.sayThisLine: The contours merge here. That's a cliff, not a trail.

payload.prompt: Tap the area on this map that looks steepest.

diagram.alt: A topographic map section showing widely spaced contours on the left, tightly bunched contours in the center, and moderately spaced contours on the right.

explanation.correct: The tightly bunched lines are a cliff. The spaced lines to the left and right are gentler slopes. Your eye should go to the packed lines first.
explanation.incorrect: Compare line spacing. Tight = steep. Spaced = gentle. This visual skill transfers to any map.

payload.prompt: Can you take a shortcut across this cliff band?

scene.alt: A topographic map showing a trail switchbacking up a slope, and a direct shortcut line across a cliff band marked with merged contours.

explanation.correct: A cliff band (merged contours) is not climbable, it is not faster and it is dangerous. The trail switchbacks for a reason: to gain elevation safely. Respect the trail.
explanation.incorrect: Shortcutting cliff bands has caused many accidents and erosion damage. Switchbacks look inefficient on a map but are the safe way up.
explanation.sayThisLine: The trail zigzags because the slope is too steep to go straight up.

payload.prompt: If you count five contours with an 80-foot interval, how much does the ground rise?

explanation.correct: 5 contours × 80 feet per contour = 400 feet of elevation gain. This is the basic math you do on the trail to estimate climb.
explanation.incorrect: Each contour crossed is one interval. Multiply the number of lines by the interval value. For steep terrain it adds up fast.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five lines at eighty feet each is four hundred feet of climbing.

lessons.title: Ridges, saddles, valleys
lessons.objective: You can pick out a ridge, saddle or drainage on a topo map.

payload.prompt: On a topo map, how do contours bend across a ridge?

options.text: They form a U or V pointing downhill
They form a U pointing uphill
They form a V pointing uphill

explanation.correct: A ridge is a spur of high ground. Contours wrap around it in a U or V that points downhill, away from the higher ground.
explanation.incorrect: Remember: contours point uphill in drainages and downhill on ridges. A V pointing uphill is a valley or stream, not a ridge.
explanation.sayThisLine: On a ridge, the contours point downhill.

payload.prompt: On a topo map, how do contours bend at a drainage?

options.text: They form a V pointing downhill
They form a U pointing uphill
They form a V pointing uphill

explanation.correct: A drainage is a valley where water flows downhill. Contours cross it in a V whose point faces uphill, upstream, toward higher ground.
explanation.incorrect: The V points upstream. A stream cuts a notch into the hillside, so the contours bend back uphill around it. On a ridge they bend the other way.
explanation.sayThisLine: That V points uphill, so it is a drainage.

payload.prompt: On a topo map, what does a saddle (pass) look like?

explanation.correct: A saddle looks like an hourglass or a bow-tie on a map. It's the low point between two higher peaks. Trails often cross at saddles because they are the lowest pass over a ridge.
explanation.incorrect: Imagine looking down at two peaks with a dip between them. The contours narrow at the low point, creating that distinctive hourglass shape.
explanation.sayThisLine: The saddle between the two peaks is where the trail crosses.

payload.prompt: Match the landform to its contour pattern.

pairs.definition: High ground; contours bend in U or V shapes pointing downhill
Valley or stream; contours form a V pointing uphill
Low point between peaks; looks like an hourglass

distractorDefinitions: A circular pattern on steep terrain

explanation.summary: Ridges and drainages are opposites. Ridge contours point downhill; drainage V's point uphill, upstream. Saddles look like hourglasses. Once you see these patterns, a topo starts to read easily.
explanation.sayThisLine: We're walking the ridge, then dropping down the spur.

payload.prompt: Tap the ridge (contours pointing downhill) on this map.

diagram.alt: A topographic map section showing three patterns: contours pointing downhill (a ridge), V shapes pointing uphill (a drainage), and an hourglass shape (a saddle).

explanation.correct: On a ridge, contours wrap around the crest and point downhill, like a tongue reaching down the slope.
explanation.incorrect: Look for contours that point downhill. Contours that V uphill mark a drainage, the opposite pattern.

lessons.title: Landforms without the flyover
lessons.objective: You can identify landforms on a static map (also the accessible path for the sim lessons).

payload.prompt: Tap the saddle (hourglass shape) on this map.

diagram.alt: A topographic map showing multiple landforms. A saddle appears as an hourglass shape between two peaks.

explanation.correct: A saddle is that narrow hourglass shape where two slopes come together and then open up again on the other side.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the pinched, hourglass shape between two higher areas. That pinch is the saddle.

payload.prompt: You see merged contours on one side of a ridge and spread-out contours on the other side. What does this mean?

options.text: One side is steep, the other is gradual
The map scale changes on each side
The ridge has a cliff on top

explanation.correct: Merged contours on one side mean a cliff or very steep drop. Spread contours mean a gentler slope. Ridges often have asymmetric sides like this.
explanation.incorrect: Terrain is often lopsided: one side might be an easy walk, the other a scramble. The map tells this story if you read the spacing.
explanation.sayThisLine: The contours are tighter on this side, so the slope has to be steeper.

payload.prompt: Tap the drainage (uphill-pointing V) on this map.

diagram.alt: A topographic map showing a ridge and a drainage. The drainage is marked by contours forming a V pointing uphill.

explanation.correct: A drainage is a valley with a V pointing uphill, upstream. Water flows down the valley, away from the point of the V.
explanation.incorrect: Compare to the ridge: ridge contours point downhill, while drainage V's point uphill. The difference is key.

payload.prompt: Which direction does water flow from a saddle between two peaks?

options.text: Down either drainage on either side
Only one direction; you have to follow the contours

explanation.correct: Rain on a saddle splits: half flows down one drainage, half down the other. A saddle is a drainage divide. This tells you where water goes from any high point.
explanation.incorrect: Understanding drainage divides is key to reading terrain. Streams follow drainages (V pointing downhill). Ridges separate drainages.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rain on a saddle splits and runs down both sides.

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: On a saddle between two peaks

facts.label: Looking at the map
facts.value: You see steep contours on one drainage, gentle on the other

options.label: Retrace the route you came up, or follow the marked trail down
options.consequence: Known, marked ground is the safest way down. Check the map at each junction as you go.
considerations: You know that ground is passable
Marked trails avoid cliff bands
If the trail is unclear, stop and use your map

options.label: Head down the gentler side, checking the map for cliffs
options.consequence: Wide contour spacing suggests easier terrain, but unmarked descents can still hit cliff bands or dead ends. Reassess often and turn back if it steepens.
considerations: Wide spacing means a gentler slope
Watch for merged contours ahead
Do not commit to ground you cannot climb back up

options.label: Go down the steep side; it will be faster
options.consequence: Steeper is not faster. It is harder to control, rough on knees, and may end at a cliff band.
considerations: Tight contours can mean cliffs
Steep descents cause falls
Slow and sure wins

payload.expertNote: Descend known, marked ground when you can. If you must choose a line, read the contours: wide spacing is gentler, merged lines are cliffs. Steeper is not faster.
payload.safetyNote: If the terrain gets steeper than you expected, stop, go back up and reassess. Off-trail descents cause many injuries.
payload.prompt: On a saddle and need to descend. One side looks steep, one gentle.

lessons.title: Three norths and declination
lessons.objective: You can explain true, magnetic and grid north and why declination matters.

payload.prompt: Match each north to what it means.

pairs.definition: The direction to the geographic North Pole; fixed
Where a compass needle points; it drifts over time
The direction of the map's vertical grid lines

distractorDefinitions: The direction the trail happens to head

explanation.summary: Three norths exist, and they differ slightly. Your compass finds magnetic north; the map is drawn to true or grid north. The difference is declination.
explanation.sayThisLine: Compass north isn't map north. Check the declination.

payload.prompt: What is declination?

options.text: The angle between true north and magnetic north
The elevation range shown on a map

explanation.correct: Declination is the angle between true north and magnetic north, where your compass points. It might be 10 degrees east in one place and 5 degrees west in another. Check the map's diagram, then confirm the current value.
explanation.incorrect: Declination varies by location and drifts a little each year, so an old map's value may be off. Ignoring it can put you hundreds of feet off course per mile.
explanation.sayThisLine: Declination here is about ten degrees east, so I adjusted.

payload.prompt: Understanding the three norths.
payload.template: A compass points to {{magnetic}} north, which differs from true north (the geographic pole). The {{angle}} between them is called {{decl}}.

explanation.correct: This is the core: compass points one way, map's grid points another, and the difference is declination. Adjust for it and you stay on course.
explanation.incorrect: Not adjusting for declination is a common source of getting turned around. Check the map's declination diagram, and confirm the current value for your area.

payload.prompt: Your map shows declination of 15 degrees west. What does that mean?

options.text: Your compass reads 15 degrees too high
Magnetic north is 15 degrees west of true north
You are 15 degrees west of the map

explanation.correct: 15 degrees west means magnetic north sits 15 degrees west of true north. To turn a map bearing into a compass bearing, add 15; to turn a compass bearing into a map bearing, subtract 15.
explanation.incorrect: Declination is printed on the map and varies by place and year. Going from map to compass, subtract east declination and add west: east is least, west is best.
explanation.sayThisLine: West declination means I add it going from map to compass.

facts.label: Question
facts.value: What bearing do you follow on your compass?

options.label: 045 - 10 = 035 degrees (subtract for east declination)
options.consequence: For east declination, subtract when turning a map bearing into a compass bearing: 45 minus 10 is 35 degrees. The compass then points where the map does.
considerations: East is least: subtract east declination
West declination gets added
Some compasses have an adjustable declination scale

options.label: 045 + 10 = 055 degrees
options.consequence: Adding when you should subtract doubles the error to 20 degrees, roughly a third of a mile off for every mile walked.
considerations: Wrong direction of correction
20 degrees is a big miss
Recheck with landmarks

options.label: Use 045 degrees as-is; declination does not matter
options.consequence: Ten degrees of ignored declination puts you roughly 900 feet off course for every mile you walk.
considerations: Small angles add up over distance
Declination varies by place
Always check it before you go

payload.expertNote: Declination is the angle between true and magnetic north, and it changes with place and year. Look up the current value. East is least, west is best: subtract east and add west when going from map bearing to compass bearing.
payload.safetyNote: Even a few degrees add up over a mile. Check the current declination for your area, and confirm your bearing with landmarks.
payload.prompt: Map bearing 045, declination 10 degrees east. What do you set?

lessons.title: Bearings and the compass
lessons.objective: You can describe how a bearing is taken and followed.

payload.prompt: Put these bearing steps in order.

items.text: Place one edge of the compass along the line you want to follow on the map
Rotate the compass dial until the orienting lines align with the map's grid lines
Read the degree number at the index line; that is your map bearing
Adjust for declination to get your compass bearing
Hold the compass level and turn your body until the red end of the needle sits inside the orienting arrow
Follow the direction-of-travel arrow: pick a landmark on that line, walk to it, and repeat

explanation.correct: This is the full sequence: map to compass to field. Skipping steps or doing them out of order is where mistakes happen.
explanation.incorrect: Each step builds on the last. Get the bearing from the map, adjust for declination, then use it to navigate.

payload.prompt: Complete the bearing basics.
payload.template: Bearings are measured {{cw}} from north: 000 is north, 090 is {{east}}, and 180 is {{south}}.

explanation.correct: Bearings are measured clockwise from north: 000 is north, 090 is east, 180 is south and 270 is west. Everything else builds from these four.
explanation.incorrect: Learn the four cardinal bearings: N is 000 or 360, E is 090, S is 180, W is 270. Bearings run clockwise from north.

payload.prompt: You take a bearing and get 225 degrees. Which direction?

explanation.correct: 225 degrees is between south (180) and west (270), so it is southwest. The pattern: 000-090 = NE quadrant, 090-180 = SE quadrant, 180-270 = SW quadrant, 270-360 = NW quadrant.
explanation.incorrect: If you are between cardinal directions, think of which two cardinals. 225 is between 180 (S) and 270 (W), so it is southwest.
explanation.sayThisLine: A bearing of two-twenty-five is southwest.

payload.prompt: A bearing of 315 degrees is which direction?

explanation.correct: 315 degrees is between west (270) and north (360). That is northwest.
explanation.incorrect: The quadrant method: 0-90 NE, 90-180 SE, 180-270 SW, 270-360 NW. 315 is in the 270-360 range, so northwest.
explanation.sayThisLine: A bearing of three-fifteen degrees is northwest.

options.label: Use the compass to stay on bearing; also use landmarks as a handrail
options.consequence: The compass keeps you honest and landmarks confirm it. If the two disagree, stop and recheck before going on.
considerations: Pick a landmark on your bearing and walk to it
Recheck often
If landmark and compass disagree, stop

options.label: Use the compass alone; ignore landmarks
options.consequence: You will hold the line, but you miss free confirmation, and errors such as a wrong declination slip through unnoticed.
considerations: Landmarks are a free second opinion
A single tool can hide mistakes
Better to use both

options.label: Ditch the compass and walk toward the mountains
options.consequence: The mountains are not a bearing. Ranges wrap around and hide, and you can drift far off your route.
considerations: Vague targets drift
You lose your route
Use the bearing you worked out

payload.expertNote: Good navigation combines compass bearings with terrain features. Use landmarks as a check on your bearing, and your bearing as a check on landmarks.
payload.safetyNote: Compass and landmarks check each other. If they disagree, stop and reassess before going any further.
payload.prompt: You have a 120-degree bearing and clear views. How do you use it?

lessons.title: Handrails and catching features
lessons.objective: You can pick a line using handrails, catching features and aiming off.

payload.prompt: What is a handrail in navigation?

options.text: A metal railing on a trail
A linear terrain feature you can follow to stay oriented

explanation.correct: A handrail is a linear feature you can follow, such as a stream, ridge, road or trail. Use only handrails your map confirms are heading the right way.
explanation.incorrect: Handrails are force multipliers: instead of checking your compass every minute, you keep a ridge, stream or trail alongside you. Confirm each one on the map first.
explanation.sayThisLine: I kept the ridge on my left as a handrail.

payload.prompt: Complete the navigation terms.
payload.template: A {{handrail}} is a feature you follow. A {{catching}} feature lies past your target and tells you that you {{overshot}}.

explanation.correct: A catching feature is a landmark beyond your target, such as a road, river or distinct ridge. If you reach it, you overshot.
explanation.incorrect: A catcher is insurance. Your target lies before it, so if you hit the catcher, stop and backtrack.

payload.prompt: Your target is a junction on a long stream. Why aim a little upstream of it?

options.text: So you know which way to turn when you hit the stream

explanation.correct: This is aiming off. If you aim right at the spot and miss by a few degrees, you will not know whether to turn up or down the stream. Aim deliberately to one side and you know which way to turn.
explanation.incorrect: Aiming off is a small deliberate error that lets you recover easily. Aim upstream so if you miss, you know to go downstream to find it.
explanation.sayThisLine: I aimed off to the left so I'd know which way to turn at the creek.

facts.label: Your goal
facts.value: Reach a trail junction marked on the map

facts.label: Options
facts.value: Bearing, or a creek the map shows

options.label: Use the creek as a handrail if the map shows it meeting the trail
options.consequence: A creek the map shows crossing your trail is a strong handrail. Confirm each landmark on the map and cross-check with your bearing.
considerations: Only use a handrail the map confirms
Note where the creek meets the trail
Do not follow a creek into unknown terrain

options.label: Follow the compass bearing and check the map often
options.consequence: A bearing works if you check it often, but in dense forest small errors pile up. Look for a handrail or landmark to confirm.
considerations: Recheck at every feature
Errors grow with distance
Add a handrail when you can

options.label: Guess the direction; you will find the trail eventually
options.consequence: Guessing in dense forest is how small errors become a lost hiker. Use the map, a bearing or a handrail.
considerations: No plan means drift
Stop and use STOP
Trails do not always connect

payload.expertNote: Handrails and bearings work best together, and each must be confirmed on the map. Creeks can lead to waterfalls, cliffs and thick brush, so only use one the map shows leading where you want to go.
payload.safetyNote: If you cannot confirm where you are, stop and use STOP. Stay on trails when you can, and do not push blindly through dense terrain.
payload.prompt: Dense forest, low visibility. How do you reach the marked junction?

lessons.title: Phone navigation done right
lessons.objective: You can prepare a phone for navigation with offline maps, tracks and waypoints.

payload.prompt: Put these phone navigation prep steps in order.

items.text: Download the offline map of your hiking area before you leave home
Drop waypoints at the trailhead, junctions, and water sources
Load a GPS track of the planned route, or create one from the map
Enable airplane mode and disable cellular to save battery
Keep your phone warm and dry, and carry a charged battery pack
Also carry a paper map and compass as backup

explanation.correct: This is the realistic preparation order. Download first (at home, on WiFi), mark landmarks, load the route, manage battery, then carry both digital and paper.
explanation.incorrect: Trying to download maps in the field on a weak signal is a recipe for getting stuck. Do it all at home.

payload.prompt: Can you count on cell signal to load maps mid-hike?

scene.alt: A phone showing no bars on a remote trail.

explanation.correct: Backcountry cell signal is spotty or absent. An offline map works without signal, so download it at home on Wi-Fi before you leave.
explanation.incorrect: Assuming you will have signal is a common navigation mistake. Prepare for no signal, and carry a paper map too.
explanation.sayThisLine: I downloaded the offline map before losing signal.

statement.speaker: She
statement.text: I saved my GPS track so I can retrace it on the way down if things get weird.

options.text: A saved track is a breadcrumb line you can follow back
She is planning for something to go wrong

payload.translation: A GPS track is a saved breadcrumb line of your path. If you get turned around, following it backward gets you out.

followUps.line: Tracks are a safety backup, but they eat battery and take time to record and view.
Modern hiker practice: load the planned track before you leave, so you can compare your progress.
A track shows where you have been, not where you are or should go.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Honestly saying 'things got weird' means you trust navigation tools and stay calm. Experts know when to lean on technology.

payload.prompt: What should you mark as waypoints?

options.text: Every tree and rock on your route
Trailhead, junctions, water sources, and landmarks

explanation.correct: Waypoints are navigation decision points and safety markers. Mark the trailhead (for returning), junctions (to confirm your route), water sources (for planning), and distant landmarks (for orientation).
explanation.incorrect: Mark only the points that matter for navigation and safety. Too many waypoints clutter your map.
explanation.sayThisLine: I dropped a waypoint at the car.

options.label: Airplane mode, screen off between checks, lean on your paper map
options.consequence: Searching for signal drains the battery fastest. Airplane mode and a dark screen stretch what is left, and a paper map needs no charge.
considerations: Airplane mode stops signal searching
Check the phone only at decision points
Carry a battery pack and keep the phone warm

options.label: Keep recording, but dim the screen and check it rarely
options.consequence: That saves some power, but the phone still hunts for signal. Add airplane mode and rely on your paper map.
considerations: Dimming helps a little
Signal searching is the big drain
Have a paper backup

options.label: Turn the phone off and navigate by memory and landmarks
options.consequence: Powering off saves battery, but memory fails after a wrong turn. A paper map and compass are the backup, not memory.
considerations: Memory is not a map
Keep the phone as a backup, not a crutch
Use paper first

payload.expertNote: Battery is your scarcest resource, and a phone is never your only map. Airplane mode, a dimmed screen and a paper backup stretch your margin.
payload.safetyNote: A dead phone is no phone. Carry a paper map and a battery pack, and plan for no signal.
payload.prompt: Two hours in, phone at 40%, no signal, GPS recording. What now?

lessons.title: Turned around? STOP
lessons.objective: You can apply STOP and dead reckoning when unsure where you are.

facts.label: You are hiking
facts.value: The terrain looks unfamiliar and junctions seem wrong

facts.label: Your first instinct
facts.value: Keep going and hope the trail turns right

options.label: STOP: sit, breathe, pull out the map and figure out where you are
options.consequence: Stopping lets you calm down, check the map, recall the last place you were sure of and choose a plan. It keeps a small mistake small.
considerations: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan
Find the last place you were sure of
Decide before you move

options.label: Backtrack a little and look for markers you missed
options.consequence: If you are confident of the way and it is not far, backtracking to your last sure point is sensible. Stop and check the map first so you do not compound the error.
considerations: Stop first, then backtrack
Go only as far as you are sure
If unsure, stay put

options.label: Push forward; trails always connect somewhere
options.consequence: Not so: keep going and you can end up farther from help, in terrain that makes recovery harder.
considerations: Trails do not always connect
Distance from help grows
Stopping is free

payload.expertNote: STOP means Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. It is your first move when unsure, and it keeps a small mistake from growing. If you cannot resolve it quickly, do not wander: stay put or call for help.
payload.safetyNote: If you are lost, injured or nightfall is near, stay put, stay warm and call 911 or text if you have signal. Blow a whistle in threes.
payload.prompt: The terrain looks unfamiliar and the junctions do not match. What now?
Put the STOP method steps in order.

items.text: Take a breath and think: when did terrain look wrong?
Observe your surroundings: landmarks, slopes, sun direction
Pull out the map and locate yourself using visible features
Decide: retrace to your last sure point, stay put, or call for help

explanation.correct: This order prevents panic and escalation. Once you are calm and oriented, you can navigate out.
explanation.incorrect: STOP is a mnemonic but the steps matter. Not observing leads to bad decisions.

payload.prompt: You hiked 40 minutes at 2 mph before realizing you were lost. How far from your last known point?

explanation.correct: Dead reckoning: 40 minutes at 2 mph is about 1.3 miles. Treat it as a rough estimate, since pace and path wander.
explanation.incorrect: Distance is speed times time: 2 mph for two thirds of an hour is about 1.3 miles. Dead reckoning is rough but useful for narrowing your search.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forty minutes at two miles an hour, so about a mile and a third along.

payload.prompt: STOP did not reveal your location. It is late, and a friend has your plan. Best move?

options.text: Run toward where you think the trail is
Follow the nearest creek downhill; it always leads out
Stay put, stay warm and visible; call 911 or text if you have signal
Keep hiking in the dark until something looks familiar

explanation.correct: Moving when lost usually makes it worse, and with your plan shared, rescuers know where to start. Stay put, layer up, make yourself visible, blow a whistle in threes, and call 911 or text if there is any signal.
explanation.incorrect: Running, following creeks and night hiking can take you into cliffs, waterfalls, brush and cold. If it is still light and you are sure of your way back, retracing to your last sure point is reasonable; otherwise stay put.
explanation.sayThisLine: If I am truly lost, I stop, stay put and call for help.

payload.prompt: You applied STOP and have your map out. You see three possible locations you could be. What is your next move?

options.text: Pick the closest one and hike there
Rule each out by matching terrain features to the map
Take a photo and text a friend
Turn on GPS and wait for a signal

explanation.correct: Use your eyes and the map to narrow down. Look at slope, vegetation, water, skyline. Which of the three possible locations matches what you see around you?
explanation.incorrect: The map and observation can pinpoint you. Use them before spending energy. If you still cannot narrow it down, treat yourself as lost: stay put and call for help.
explanation.sayThisLine: When I get turned around, I do STOP. Sit, breathe, look at the map.
